title: Effects of Z-seam mitigation on energy absorption and dimensional accuracy of printed circular tubes
abstract: Abstract In Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF), the Z-seam is the start–stop discontinuity formed at the beginning and end of each deposited perimeter, degrades both dimensional accuracy and crash energy absorption by acting as a stress concentration and tear-initiation site. This study quantitatively assesses advanced mitigation strategies to simultaneously optimize dimensional fidelity and crashworthiness in ABS circular tubes. Seam modification strategies comprising Pressure Advance to compensate for nozzle pressure lag and the Scarf Joint seam to replace abrupt steps with tapered overlaps were evaluated individually and in combination. Seam placement using Aligned, Back, and Nearest positions was controlled via a full factorial design of twelve build conditions. Quasi-static axial compression tests quantified energy absorption metrics, while full-field 3D scan-to-CAD analysis quantified dimensional deviation and oversize. Pressure Advance increased stiffness by stabilizing extrusion flow, whereas the Scarf Joint redistributed the seam discontinuity, reduced peak force, and promoted progressive folding. Seam placement strongly governed energy absorption where Back placement consistently outperformed other configurations. The combined Pressure Advance–Scarf Joint configuration with Back seam placement achieved the optimal multi-objective response, delivering a SEA of 16.95 kJ kg⁻ 1 , EA of 23.50 daJ, and CFE of 50.96%, while also exhibiting the high dimensional compliance. To resolve trade-offs between geometric accuracy and mechanical performance, a hybrid framework integrating two-way ANOVA and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied. SHAP attribution revealed that seam placement governed absorbed energy variance, whereas seam modification dominated stiffness and crush force efficiency, establishing Z-seam control as an optimization-ready design variable for crashworthy FFF components.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Material Extrusion (MEX), a category of additive manufacturing (AM) processes, has become one of the most widely adopted technologies for fabricating parts from thermoplastic polymers and composites [ 1 ]. This prevalence is largely due to the technology’s low initial investment, operational simplicity, and compatibility with a broad range of materials. The most common MEX process is known by the trademarked term Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), a process in which a thermoplastic filament is fed from a spool, heated to a semi-molten state within a liquefier, and extruded through a nozzle. The part is constructed layer-by-layer as the nozzle deposits material onto a build platform, with its path precisely controlled by a digital model [ 2 ].

Initially developed for rapid prototyping, the application space for FDM has expanded dramatically. It is now increasingly utilized for the production of functional, end-use components in demanding sectors such as aerospace, automotive, and healthcare [ 3 ]. This transition from producing form-and-fit prototypes to manufacturing engineering-grade parts has intensified the need for components with reliable and predictable properties [ 4 ]. To achieve this, a systematic optimization of process parameters is required to strike an ideal balance between two primary objectives: robust mechanical properties and high dimensional accuracy [ 5 ].

The fabrication of components with strong mechanical performance presents a multi-faceted engineering challenge that requires a comprehensive methodology, integrating advancements across material science, printer technology advancements, process parameter optimisation, and post-processing techniques [ 6 ]. In the realm of material science, this includes the development of high-performance engineering thermoplastics and composite filaments reinforced with short or continuous fibers to drastically improve stiffness and tensile strength [ 7 ]. Furthermore, multi-material printing enables the fabrication of complex components by combining polymers with distinct properties within a single part [ 8 ]. The potential of these materials is then realized through meticulous process optimisation. Key parameters such as infill density and type [ 9 ], line height [ 10 ] and line width [ 11 ], print orientation [ 12 ], and thermal factors like extrusion temperature [ 13 ] are manipulated to promote strong interlaminar adhesion. Finally, upon completion of printing, post-processing methods like thermal annealing [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ] can further augment performance by relieving internal stresses and improving the final part’s strength and stability.

The second core challenge is the attainment of both high dimensional accuracy and a superior, defect-free surface finish, which is critical for any component requiring tight tolerances and consistent geometric fidelity. Dimensional accuracy refers to the degree to which the final printed object conforms to its Computer-Aided Design (CAD) model [ 17 ]. Geometric inconsistencies are commonly introduced through material shrinkage [ 18 ], thermal gradients [ 19 ], and characteristic print artifacts such as the stairstep effect on sloped surfaces [ 20 ], base-layer bulging known as elephant’s foot [ 21 ], localized defects like blobs and zits, and the Z-seam [ 22 ].

Mitigating these issues begins with the printer’s hardware and technology. A rigid mechanical frame with a precise motion system is an essential prerequisite for repeatability[ 23 ], while advancements like closed-loop stepper motors can correct for positional errors in real-time [ 24 ]. Stable thermal control, typically achieved via an enclosed and actively heated build chamber, is also crucial for minimizing and normalizing material shrinkage, particularly for engineering-grade polymers [ 25 ].

Slicing parameter optimization remains one of the most effective and accessible strategies. For instance, lower layer heights reduce the visual and dimensional impact of the staircase effect, while precise calibration of the material flow rate prevents over- or under-extrusion that leads to blobs and dimensional error [ 26 ]. The Z-seam, caused by the pressure dynamics of starting and stopping extrusion, can be carefully managed through strategic placement on sharp corners or non-critical surfaces to hide its appearance [ 27 ].

Finally, post-processing techniques improve the final dimensional accuracy and surface quality. Subtractive methods like precision sanding can eliminate visual discontinuities such as layer lines and seam artifacts [ 28 ]. Conversely, additive methods like coating or vapor smoothing can be applied to create a uniform, smooth finish, completing the process of producing an engineering-grade component [ 29 ].

The Z-seam, an inherent discontinuity in parts produced by FDM, is not merely a cosmetic artifact but a critical feature that impacts dimensional accuracy and mechanical performance [ 27 ]. It introduces a geometric imperfection acting as a stress concentration point that can initiate failure under load. While slicing software allows for seam placement and perimeter tuning to manage trade-offs between surface finish and precision, these strategies are largely ineffective for cylindrical geometries which lack sharp corners to conceal the discontinuity. On such curved surfaces, the seam’s detrimental effects on aesthetics, local accuracy, and structural reliability are magnified. Despite various empirical mitigation strategies, a comprehensive quantitative understanding of the Z-seam’s coupled influence across mechanical and dimensional domains remains underexplored. Addressing this gap is essential for developing the predictive models required to transition FDM from a prototyping tool to a method for industrial-grade production.

This issue becomes especially critical in the design of energy-absorbing structures, such as automotive crash boxes, which are engineered to convert kinetic energy into plastic deformation during an impact. Thin-walled circular tubes are widely favored for these applications due to their predictable, symmetric deformation behavior and high energy absorption efficiency [ 30 ]. However, the presence of a Z-seam introduces a significant geometric discontinuity, creating a preferential site for stress concentration and failure initiation under the compressive loads characteristic of a crash event. This seam-induced imperfection threatens to undermine the otherwise superior performance of circular cross-sections in safety–critical applications [ 31 ]. Indeed, previous studies investigating FDM-fabricated circular hollow tubes have reported a wide range of failure modes that are strongly dependent on the material system, reinforcement strategy, and seam-related defects. For instance, quasi-static compression tests on PETG reinforced with short carbon fibers revealed that the majority of specimens failed directly at the Z-seam location, where crack initiation and subsequent propagation occurred along the vertical seam line [ 31 ]. Similarly, investigations on PLA circular tubes incorporating an internal concentric ring reported vertical tearing during compression, indicating the presence of dominant axial weakness paths attributed to the manufacturing process [ 32 ]. Conversely, studies on polyamide (PA) tubes reinforced with glass and carbon fibers demonstrated more stable collapse behaviors; glass fiber–reinforced PA exhibited largely progressive deformation with limited Euler-type buckling, while carbon fiber–reinforced PA showed a stable progressive folding mode [ 33 ]. Additional work on circular tubes fabricated from various PLA grades (PLA + , PLA-ST, PLA-LW, PLA-CF), PETG, and ABS has also reported predominantly progressive folding behavior despite the presence of unmodified Z-seams [ 30 ,  34 ]. Collectively, these observations indicate that while progressive collapse is achievable in FDM-printed circular tubes, the Z-seam remains a governing factor in failure initiation, often introducing critical variability that compromises the reliability required for energy-absorbing applications.

Therefore, a systematic evaluation of the Z-seam’s influence on the structural integrity of such components is imperative. Investigating the effect of Z-seam through quasi-static axial compression testing is vital to characterizing its impact on deformation behavior and failure mechanisms. The insights gained will be essential for developing optimized slicing strategies and design guidelines to enhance the reliability of FDM-produced parts in load-bearing and safety–critical contexts.

This work explores strategies for minimizing the Z-seam to enhance the dimensional accuracy of manufactured components. To evaluate the influence of a reduced z-seam on both dimensional precision and energy absorption capacity, thin-walled circular tubes were subjected to quasi-static compression tests. This geometry was strategically chosen because circular profiles are not only known for their high energy absorption performance, but their continuous, cornerless surface makes z-seam defects more prominent and impossible to conceal [ 27 ,  33 ].

The development of Z-seam management features in 3D printing slicers has been a continuous evolution driven by the need for improved surface quality and mechanical performance. The evolution of Z-seam management in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) has been marked by progressive refinements in both slicing software and printer firmware, aimed at improving surface quality, dimensional precision, and mechanical integrity. Consequently, the management of Z seam discontinuities has evolved from rudimentary placement controls to sophisticated firmware and geometric solutions. While early slicing strategies focused on concealing the seam via spatial alignment or randomization, significant improvements arose from firmware level algorithms specifically Pressure Advance and Linear Advance which modulate extrusion to counter nozzle pressure lag. Most recently, geometric strategies such as the Scarf Joint have been implemented to replace abrupt layer transitions with tapered overlaps, shifting Z seam management from a cosmetic fix to a functional design parameter.

From the various Z-seam improvement methods available, this study assesses the efficacy of three prominent techniques: seam positioning (back, aligned, nearest), Pressure Advance, and the Scarf Joint Seam. The research quantifies the influence of these methods on key part characteristics, including dimensional accuracy, surface topology, and compressive mechanical properties.

Seam positioning is a fundamental slicer process that dictates the location of the Z-seam by strategically placing the start and end point of each layer’s external perimeter. Common placement strategies include Back, which fixes the seam to the back of the build plate; Aligned, which stacks all points into a single vertical line; and Nearest, which attempts to hide the seam on the closest available geometric corner. The chosen strategy is critical for managing the final aesthetic and mechanical properties of the part.

Pressure Advance, and its equivalent Linear Advance in Marlin firmware, is a predictive firmware-level algorithm designed to compensate for the dynamic effects of pressure within the printer’s hotend. In a standard FDM system, the molten polymer acts as a compressible fluid that creates a viscoelastic lag between the extruder gear motion and the actual nozzle output. This hysteresis typically results in excess pressure and blobs when the nozzle decelerates at the end of a seam, and a pressure deficit or gap when it accelerates at the start. Pressure Advance proactively modulates the filament feed rate by pressurizing the nozzle before acceleration and relieving pressure before deceleration. This process ensures the extrusion flow consistently matches the nozzle velocity and effectively eliminates these start-stop artifacts.

The Scarf Joint Seam is a geometric slicing strategy that fundamentally alters the seam topology by drawing inspiration from the overlapping joinery method used in woodworking. While a traditional Z-seam forms an abrupt butt joint where the perimeter start and end points meet vertically to create a distinct weak point, the scarf joint replaces this with a sloped, overlapping interface. The slicer achieves this by tapering the extrusion path so that the nozzle ramps the flow down to a thin taper at the end of a loop and ramps it up at the start of the next. This blended transition eliminates the sharp vertical discontinuity and distributes the bond over a larger surface area, which significantly improves both surface continuity and mechanical integrity.

Despite the Z-seam’s recognized impact on dimensional accuracy, surface topology, and mechanical properties, its comprehensive influence remains underexplored in the academic literature. A range of studies has explored basic z-seam mitigation strategies through parameter optimization, material design, and structural control. Irimia et al. [ 27 ] systematically investigated the effect of slicer parameters Z Seam Alignment (ZSA), Seam Corner Preference (SCP), Outer Wall Wipe Distance (WD), and Coasting Volume (CV) and demonstrated that strategic tuning of these inputs can substantially reduce seam area and improve visual quality. Their work highlighted a trade-off: while certain configurations minimized seam size, others better concealed the seam for improved appearance, emphasizing the importance of tailoring settings to application-specific requirements. Similarly, Aguirre et al. [ 21 ] integrated z-seam control into a printer-specific profiling procedure. By aligning the z-seam to the sharpest corner and enabling the coasting feature, they reduced dimensional inaccuracies, particularly in cylindrical parts. Other researchers have addressed the z-seam from a mechanical integrity standpoint. Chafik et al. identified the z-seam as a consistent failure site under tensile loading at higher print temperatures, recommending its relocation to low-stress regions such as corners to avoid premature failure [ 35 ]. Likewise, Economides et al. observed that z-seam discontinuities acted as crack initiation sites in carbon-fiber-reinforced Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol (PETG) specimens during compression, reinforcing the need for seam-aware design and slicing strategies to enhance structural performance [ 31 ]. Beyond parameter tuning, material formulation has also proven effective in reducing z-seam defects. Liu et al. found that blending Polylactic Acid (PLA) into Ethylene Vinyl Acetate (EVA) significantly decreased z-seam area and width in both cubic and toroidal models. Improvements were most pronounced up to 5% PLA content, beyond which benefits plateaued demonstrating that modest material modifications can notably enhance surface quality by improving flow stability and interlayer adhesion [ 36 ]. Not all studies viewed the z-seam as a flaw to eliminate. Shim and Hou reframed it as a diagnostic tool, showing that the periodic patterns of z-seams serve as “fingerprints” of slicer behavior. Different slicing programs were found to produce distinct seam patterns, providing a forensic pathway to identify slicer origin or detect process inconsistencies. This perspective introduces a novel functional role for the z-seam in validating prints and tracing digital provenance in additive manufacturing workflows [ 37 ]. In some cases, rather than optimizing the z-seam, researchers chose to control and standardize its position to ensure reliable experimental results. For instance, Tamaşag et al., investigating in-process filament colouring, fixed the seam location to prevent it from skewing tensile and surface roughness measurements an approach that underscores the z-seam’s capacity to introduce variability even in unrelated research domains [ 38 ]. Lastly, Weflen and Frank, in developing a hybrid additive–subtractive system for fabricating polymer-metal components, encountered z-seam over-extrusion issues at longer layer times. By adjusting the pre-start delay before extrusion, they minimized excess deposition at the seam, achieving better surface uniformity and dimensional accuracy. Their work further demonstrated the value of geometry-dependent, dynamic parameter tuning to manage seam formation in complex or large-scale prints [ 39 ]. Collectively, these studies reveal that the z-seam is far more than a superficial printing artifact. It plays a pivotal role across aesthetic quality, structural reliability, material-process interaction, and digital traceability, warranting deliberate attention in both research and practice.

Systematic investigations into advanced Z-seam mitigation strategies and their broader impact on print performance remain limited. One of the earliest academic studies on pressure compensation, Tronvoll et al. introduced and validated the Linear Advance 1.0 algorithm in Marlin firmware, targeting extrusion defects during print head acceleration and deceleration. Using an Original Prusa i3 MK2.5 and PLA at three layer heights (0.10, 0.20, 0.30 mm), they found that lower layer heights required significantly higher compensation values, with the optimal value at 0.1 mm nearly double that of 0.3 mm. The results closely aligned with a Simulink simulation, supporting the theoretical model’s validity [ 40 ]. Expanding on pressure control for dimensional accuracy, Grgić et al. calibrated a Creality Ender-3 Pro for functional FDM assemblies using ISO 286-1:2010 tolerancing. They applied a Linear Advance factor of 25 and optimized Hole Horizontal Expansion (HHE) to 0.13 mm, improving internal feature accuracy. Additionally, a CAD strategy based on the arithmetic mean of tolerance bounds yielded clearance fits tighter than standards. The study demonstrated how combining extrusion tuning, slicer compensation, and design-level adjustments can enhance precision in low-cost systems [ 41 ]. In a more automated context, Al Nabhani et al. developed a machine-to-machine calibration framework using machine vision to optimize pressure advance in real time. A high-end “instrumented” printer with a 3D scanner determined optimal parameters by analyzing calibration beads, then transferred the adjusted G-code to a standard “production” printer. Tested on a ball valve component, the system successfully corrected over- and under-extrusion defects seen in uncalibrated prints. Their work highlights a scalable, Industry 4.0-compatible approach for improving extrusion quality across networked FDM platforms [ 42 ].

While existing literature indicates that firmware features like Linear Advance and Pressure Advance can enhance product quality and dimensional accuracy in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), a comprehensive understanding of their effects on engineering-grade materials and specific mechanical applications remains limited. Therefore, this study investigates the impact of various Z-seam improvement techniques on parts fabricated from Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS). This engineering thermoplastic was selected for its high glass transition temperature and toughness, making it a viable candidate for energy-absorbing structures such as crash boxes. To this end, thin-walled circular tubes were manufactured using these different techniques, and their dimensional accuracy and surface topology were characterized. The specimens were then subjected to quasi-static axial compression tests to evaluate how each Z-seam improvement strategy influences their resulting energy absorption performance and failure modes. Finally, the experimental dataset was systematically analyzed using a two-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) to determine whether the effects of Z-seam distribution and modification strategies are statistically distinguishable from experimental scatter, with main effects and interaction plots employed to elucidate directional trends and factor interplay. To complement this variance-based inference and to interrogate the explainable structure of the measured responses, a SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis built on gradient-boosted regression models was further applied to quantify relative parameter importance and resolve potentially non-linear influences on the mechanical performance that may not be statistically resolvable through ANOVA alone.

sections.heading: Design and fabrication of ABS circular thin-wall structure
paragraphs: This study investigates the energy absorption performance of circular cross-section structures featuring a visually improved z-seam. First, the hollow structure was designed using CAD software. The tubular geometry was defined with an outer diameter of 30 mm, a wall thickness of 2 mm and a height of 80 mm.

The specimens were fabricated using a Bambu Lab P1S fused filament fabrication system equipped with a 0.4 mm stainless steel nozzle. A commercial white Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene filament with a nominal diameter of 1.75 mm (ABG, Turkey) was used throughout the study. To ensure a consistent and reproducible baseline print quality prior to investigating Z-seam strategies, a systematic pre-calibration procedure was carried out using the integrated calibration tools of Orca Slicer and widely adopted open-source calibration geometries.

Calibration was performed using parameter-specific calibration towers, defined as vertically segmented test specimens in which a single process parameter is varied stepwise along the build height while all other parameters are kept constant. This approach enables direct comparison of printing outcomes under identical environmental and geometric conditions. The calibration procedure included nozzle temperature calibration, build plate temperature evaluation, printing speed optimization, extrusion multiplier calibration, and retraction distance and speed optimization.

For nozzle temperature calibration, a temperature tower spanning 220–240 °C in 5 °C increments was printed in accordance with the filament manufacturer’s recommended processing window. The optimal temperature was selected based on visual inspection of interlayer bonding, surface uniformity, and the absence of under-extrusion or excessive surface gloss associated with overheating. A nozzle temperature of 235 °C provided the best balance between layer adhesion and surface finish and was therefore adopted. Given the susceptibility of ABS to warping and inadequate bed adhesion, build plate temperature was evaluated independently by printing identical test geometries at 80, 90, and 100 °C. The selection criterion was complete first-layer adhesion without edge lifting or corner warping. A bed temperature of 100 °C was found to be the most effective and was used for all subsequent prints. Printing speed was calibrated using a speed tower in which the nominal print speed was varied from 30 to 80 mm/s in 10 mm/s increments. The selection criterion was the preservation of geometric fidelity and surface quality, assessed visually and by confirming the absence of ringing, vibration artifacts, or under-extrusion. A printing speed of 40 mm/s yielded the most consistent surface quality and dimensional stability and was therefore selected. The extrusion multiplier was calibrated using a dedicated flow rate test structure with extrusion multiplier values ranging from 0.94 to 1.00 in increments of 0.02. The optimal value was determined through visual assessment of surface texture and line overlap, with the explicit objective of avoiding over-extrusion manifested as ridging or material buildup. An extrusion multiplier of 0.98 produced uniform extrusion and well-defined perimeters and was adopted. Retraction behavior was optimized to minimize stringing and oozing using a retraction test geometry. Retraction distance was varied between 0.6 and 1.2 mm in 0.2 mm increments, while retraction speed was varied from 25 to 45 mm/s in 5 mm/s increments. The optimal values were identified through visual inspection of stringing between features and the absence of extrusion delays at restart points. A retraction distance of 0.8 mm and a retraction speed of 30 mm/s provided the best overall performance. In addition, the part cooling fan speed was fixed at 25% for all prints to balance layer adhesion and surface stability when processing ABS. All calibrated parameters, including nozzle temperature of 235 °C, build plate temperature of 100 °C, printing speed of 40 mm/s, extrusion multiplier of 0.98, retraction distance of 0.8 mm, retraction speed of 30 mm/s, and cooling fan speed of 25%, were held constant for the fabrication of all specimens. This ensured that differences observed in the Z-seam analysis originated from seam placement strategies rather than variations in baseline printing conditions.

The optimal Pressure Advance value was identified through a multi-stage calibration process using the integrated routines within Orca Slicer. The calibration began by defining a start point, an end point, and a specific step increment for the pressure advance coefficient. The PA Line test was first executed to print a series of straight lines where each individual line corresponded to a distinct PA value within this defined range. This visual assessment allowed for the selection of the specific line that yielded the most uniform extrusion free of defects. Subsequently, the PA Pattern method was employed to print a series of 90° corners. Similar to the line test, each corner feature in this pattern was printed with a different PA value based on the pre-defined range and step to identify the setting that produced the sharpest vertices with the fewest gaps or bulges. Finally, a PA Tower was printed for fine-grained analysis using a hollow pentagonal structure where the PA value changed continuously along the  z -axis. The height of the region displaying optimal quality was measured and multiplied by a factor of 0.002 to derive the final firmware coefficient for the direct-drive extruder. This empirically derived value (0.0265) was then applied to the filament profile to compensate for nozzle pressure hysteresis during acceleration and deceleration.

The Scarf Joint Seam was applied to both inner and outer perimeter walls by configuring the slicer to generate a tapered interface. To maximize the available bonding surface area while maintaining geometric fidelity on the 30 mm diameter curvature, a scarf length of 20 mm with 10 steps was selected. This configuration directed the nozzle to taper the extrusion path via downward and upward sloping ramps at the loop’s start and end points. This process created a blended, overlapping transition that distributed the discontinuity across a larger surface area rather than forming a standard vertical butt joint. Following production, all specimens underwent a rigorous visual inspection to identify imperfections such as voids or cracks, and any defective samples were excluded from testing.

To systematically evaluate the effects of different printing parameters, the hollow tubes were fabricated in twelve unique configurations. This experimental design combined four distinct feature enhancement groups with three different seam placement options. The enhancement groups consisted of specimens printed with Pressure Advance only, with a Scarf Joint seam only, with both features applied simultaneously, and a baseline group with neither improvement. Each of these groups was then printed using Back, Aligned, and Nearest seam placements, creating a full factorial study to assess the individual and combined effects of these settings. For each of these 12 cases, three identical specimens were produced for quasi-static compression testing, leading to a total of 36 test samples. The complete full factorial experimental design, distinguishing Z-seam strategies by their underlying control mechanisms and defining the corresponding alphanumeric nomenclature, is summarized in Table  1 . sections.heading: Experimental procedure and visual examination
paragraphs: Quasi-static compression tests were performed using a Shimadzu Universal Testing Machine equipped with a 100 kN load cell. Following the ASTM D695 standard, a constant compression speed of 1.6 mm/min was applied. Throughout each test, force–displacement data were recorded at 20 Hz, and images of the deformation were captured at 11.2 mm intervals up to a total displacement of 56 mm.

After fabrication, specimens were scanned to analyze their geometry using a Moose 3D Scanner. The scanner was configured for an accuracy of 0.03 mm, a resolution of 0.07 mm, and a frame rate of 10 fps. For the procedure, each tube was placed on a rotational table while the scanner was positioned at a fixed distance of 160 mm. The scanned data was then imported into free trial version of Geomagic Control X software. A mesh-to-CAD comparison was conducted by aligning the scanned data with the original CAD model of the tubes. This process served to quantitatively evaluate the manufacturing accuracy and identify any dimensional deviations from the nominal design.

sections.heading: Energy absorption performance metrics and results evaluation
paragraphs: The energy absorption capacity of materials is a pivotal parameter in applications requiring impact mitigation and crashworthiness. This characteristic is most effectively quantified through quasi-static compression testing, wherein a specimen is compressed at a constant, low velocity between a stationary and a moving platen. During this process, force and displacement are continuously recorded, yielding a force–displacement curve that encapsulates the material’s mechanical response under load. This curve typically exhibits four distinct regions, as illustrated in Fig.  1 . The initial region corresponds to linear elastic deformation, characterized by a steep increase in force with minimal displacement. This response is governed primarily by the material’s stiffness and the elastic bending of its microstructural features, such as tube walls. The termination of this region is marked by the Peak Crushing Force (PCF), signifying the yield point and the onset of irreversible deformation. Fig. 1 Force–displacement curve regions [ 43 ]

Beyond the PCF lies the plateau region, which is the most critical for energy absorption. In this phase, the force remains relatively constant while the specimen undergoes significant deformation via progressive folding, buckling, or crushing. The morphology of the plateau whether smooth or oscillatory reflects the underlying crushing mechanism and structural instabilities of the material. A long, stable plateau indicates sustained energy dissipation with controlled deformation [ 44 ].

As the material structure collapses and internal voids are eliminated, the response transitions into the densification region, characterized by a sharp increase in force with minimal additional displacement. Here, opposing material surfaces are in direct contact, resulting in rapidly increasing resistance to further compression [ 45 ].

An ideal energy-absorbing material exhibits a low PCF to reduce initial impact loads and a long, stable plateau to maximize energy dissipation before densification. The total energy absorbed is represented by the area under the force–displacement curve. This area is maximized when the plateau region features extensive folding or crush events, indicating a high capacity for controlled and progressive energy dissipation [ 46 ].

An ideal energy-absorbing structure should exhibit a low PCF to minimize initial impact severity, followed by a high and stable MCF that enables sustained energy dissipation through progressive deformation. The combination of high EA, high SEA, and CFE approaching unity indicates excellent crashworthiness, particularly in weight-sensitive applications. Moreover, achieving optimal crash performance requires balanced stiffness. Overly stiff structures may fail catastrophically or transmit high loads to adjacent components, compromising safety. Conversely, structures with inadequate stiffness may undergo premature collapse without sufficient energy dissipation. Therefore, the most effective designs possess moderate stiffness, enabling controlled deformation mechanisms such as plastic folding, buckling, or progressive crushing while maintaining structural integrity and maximizing energy absorption efficiency [ 48 ].

The results of the quasi-static compression tests were systematically analyzed using established performance metrics. These results are presented in the form of bar charts, with error bars representing the standard deviation to illustrate data variability and experimental repeatability. To ensure clarity and facilitate meaningful comparisons, the mechanical performance associated with each z-seam modification is individually highlighted in the graphs. This visualization approach provides a comprehensive and intuitive understanding of how z-seam positioning influences key crashworthiness parameters. This methodology facilitates a comprehensive comparative analysis of seven key performance indicators: Mean Crushing Force (MCF), Peak Crushing Force (PCF), Total Absorbed Energy, Specific Energy Absorption (SEA), Stiffness, Maximum Stress and Crushing Force Efficiency (CFE). To improve data clarity and allow for direct comparison, performance indicators were grouped into two separate graphs based on their numerical magnitude. The first graph consolidates the force and stiffness metrics, displaying Mean Crushing Force (MCF) and Peak Crushing Force-Max Force (PCF) in Newtons (N), and Stiffness in Newtons per millimeter (N/mm). The second graph presents the remaining metrics, including Specific Energy Absorption (SEA) in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg), Total Absorbed Energy in decajoules (daJ), Maximum Stress in megapascals (MPa), Mass in grams (g), and Crushing Force Efficiency (CFE) as a percentage (%). To track each configuration, a systematic nomenclature was adopted to designate specimens based on their specific z-seam improvement method. A systematic nomenclature was adopted to designate each specimen by encoding its specific configuration. This alphanumeric code’s final letter denotes the seam location: A for Aligned, N for Nearest, and B for Back. The initial letters in the code identify the z-seam improvement method used: N indicates that neither pressure advance nor a scarf joint seam was applied, S denotes a Scarf joint seam, P signifies that pressure advance was applied, and P–S means both pressure advance and a scarf joint seam were utilized together.

Figure  2  presents the variation in stiffness (N/mm), mean crushing force (MCF, N), and peak crushing force-max force (PCF, N) across specimens fabricated with different z-seam improvement methods and seam locations. Fig. 2 Stiffness, MCF, and PCF variations across Z-seam modification methods

The results clearly demonstrate that both Z-seam modification strategies and seam placement exert a decisive influence on specimen stiffness, which governs not only the elastic response but also the initiation and stability of progressive collapse in energy-absorbing structures. The application of Pressure Advance (P) consistently increased stiffness, producing a more rigid structure. This behavior can be attributed to improved extrusion pressure regulation, which enhances interlayer bonding continuity and reduces void formation at the seam, thereby increasing effective load transfer in the elastic regime. Conversely, the Scarf Joint (S) modification noticeably decreased stiffness relative to the baseline, as the tapered seam geometry intentionally disrupts axial material continuity, introducing localized compliance that facilitates early deformation. Within each modification group, the Nearest seam location consistently resulted in the lowest stiffness values, reflecting the detrimental effect of concentrating geometric discontinuities within high-stress regions directly engaged during axial loading.

In the context of energy absorption, neither extreme stiffness nor excessive flexibility is desirable. Overly stiff structures tend to exhibit unstable or brittle collapse, characterized by high peak forces and limited folding, whereas excessively compliant structures collapse prematurely with insufficient resistance, resulting in poor energy dissipation. Consequently, a moderate stiffness level is required to promote controlled, progressive folding. The combined Pressure Advance–Scarf Joint (PS) configuration provides this balanced response, yielding stiffness values lower than the rigid P group yet higher than the flexible S group. This intermediate stiffness enables stable fold initiation while preserving sufficient load-bearing capacity throughout collapse. Accordingly, a configuration such as P–S–A (Pressure Advance + Scarf Joint with Aligned seam) represents an effective engineering compromise, achieving a favorable balance between structural rigidity and deformability that is essential for crashworthy energy-absorbing components.

Peak Crushing Force (PCF) trends further reinforce this interpretation. In crashworthiness applications, a lower PCF is desirable, as high initial forces correspond to greater impact loads transmitted to occupants. The unmodified baseline specimens, particularly N–B, exhibited the highest and therefore least favorable PCF values. In contrast, the Scarf Joint modification proved most effective in reducing peak force. This reduction arises from the seam’s ability to act as a controlled deformation trigger, smoothing force build-up during collapse initiation. While Pressure Advance and the combined PS strategy also reduced PCF relative to the baseline, their effect was less pronounced, reflecting the competing influence of increased material continuity on peak load formation. With respect to seam placement, the Back location consistently produced higher PCF values, as fold initiation is delayed when the seam is shielded from the primary loading face, whereas the Nearest location yielded the lowest peak forces by promoting earlier instability.

Mean Crushing Force (MCF) provides a complementary measure of sustained energy absorption capability, as higher MCF values indicate the structure’s ability to maintain load throughout progressive collapse. Several configurations exhibit superior performance in this regard, notably PS–B and P–B, as well as S–A. These results suggest that once collapse is initiated, enhanced interlayer cohesion from Pressure Advance allows the structure to sustain higher average loads, particularly when combined with seam placements that delay catastrophic fracture. Collectively, these findings indicate that optimal crashworthy performance in FDM-fabricated ABS structures is achieved not by maximizing any single response, but by strategically tuning Z-seam geometry and placement to balance stiffness, peak force mitigation, and sustained crushing resistance a design principle directly relevant to lightweight crash boxes and energy-absorbing structural components.

Figure  3  evaluates the remaining performance metrics of the energy-absorbing structures, including their weight and mechanical properties. Fig. 3 Variations in mass, SEA, absorbed energy, maximum stress, and CFE across Z-seam modification methods

All specimens were weighed prior to testing, with dimensional consistency ensured across the dataset. Specimens fabricated with a Scarf Joint seam exhibited systematically lower mass than the other configurations, which is directly attributable to the suppression of material bulging and blob formation at the Z-seam. By redistributing the seam over an inclined interface, the Scarf Joint reduces localized over-extrusion and excess filament accumulation. This localized mass reduction is mechanically relevant, as it simultaneously decreases local stiffness at the seam region, creating a compliant trigger that alters the onset and evolution of collapse. Consequently, specimens incorporating the Scarf Joint exhibit lower initial rigidity than their non-scarf counterparts, an effect that directly influences subsequent energy absorption behavior.

For Total Absorbed Energy (EA), where higher values correspond to improved crashworthiness, the results identify clear top-performing configurations. The specimen combining both modifications with a Back seam (PS–B) achieved the highest absorbed energy (23.50 daJ), closely followed by the Pressure Advance–Back configuration (P–B). This trend highlights Pressure Advance as a primary contributor to energy dissipation, as improved pressure regulation enhances interlayer bonding and enables sustained load transfer during progressive folding. In contrast, the S–N (Scarf–Nearest) specimen absorbed the least energy, indicating that excessive compliance combined with an unfavorable seam location leads to premature collapse and limited resistance during deformation.

Specific Energy Absorption (SEA), which normalizes energy absorption by specimen mass and is therefore critical for lightweight structural design, further clarifies the interaction between processing strategies. While Pressure Advance (P) and the Scarf Joint (S) produced limited improvements when applied independently, their combined application resulted in a clear synergistic enhancement of SEA, with PS–B achieving the highest value (16.95 kJ/kg). This synergy arises because Pressure Advance compensates for the local compliance introduced by the Scarf Joint, producing a seam that is both geometrically smooth and structurally dense. Seam location plays a decisive role, with the Back position consistently enhancing SEA, likely due to delayed seam engagement during folding, whereas the Nearest position yields the lowest values by concentrating structural discontinuities in highly stressed regions.

Peak Crushing Force (PCF), which directly correlates with maximum stress transmitted during impact, provides further insight into crashworthiness performance. Because excessively high PCF values are undesirable from a safety perspective, an optimal structure must balance peak force reduction with sustained load capacity. The unmodified baseline specimens exhibited the highest and least favorable PCF values. Both Pressure Advance and the Scarf Joint significantly reduced PCF, with the Scarf Joint showing a more pronounced effect due to its ability to blunt the initial force peak by introducing a controlled deformation zone. Notably, the combined P–S configuration produced an intermediate PCF lower than the baseline yet higher than the Scarf-only case indicating a deliberate moderation of force transmission rather than an uncontrolled reduction in resistance. This behavior reflects a desirable compromise between safety and structural integrity.

Crushing Force Efficiency (CFE), defined as the ratio of Mean Crushing Force (MCF) to PCF, captures the stability of the force–displacement response. Higher CFE values indicate a more uniform crushing process with reduced force oscillations. Both Pressure Advance and Scarf Joint modifications improved CFE, with the Scarf Joint exerting the stronger individual influence. A clear synergistic effect emerges when both strategies are combined, yielding the highest CFE values, particularly for PS–B, followed by S–A. This improvement confirms that combined seam smoothing and pressure regulation promote a more ideal collapse mode, characterized by sustained resistance without excessive initial force spikes.

Taken together, the combined analysis of stiffness, EA, SEA, PCF, MCF, and CFE demonstrates that Z-seam mitigation strategies influence crashworthiness primarily by altering seam morphology, local stiffness, and fold initiation behavior. Pressure Advance enhances interlayer cohesion and structural rigidity, increasing MCF and total energy absorption, but at the cost of elevated PCF if applied alone. Conversely, the Scarf Joint reduces mass and stiffness, suppresses peak forces, and promotes early folding, but may limit total energy dissipation if not compensated. The combined P–S strategy reconciles these competing effects, yielding moderate stiffness, reduced PCF, high MCF, and the highest SEA through stable, progressive folding. Two distinct interaction modes are observed: synergistic interactions, such as for CFE and SEA, where combined modifications outperform individual strategies, and balancing interactions, where opposing effects produce intermediate performance. Seam placement further modulates these mechanisms, with the Back location consistently enhancing performance through geometric shielding, while the Nearest location introduces structural weaknesses that degrade response. Ultimately, integrating Pressure Advance and Scarf Joint modifications particularly with a Back seam placement emerges as the most effective strategy for maximizing energy absorption, crashworthiness, and lightweight efficiency in FDM-fabricated ABS structures.

sections.heading: Deformation modes
paragraphs: In structural mechanics, axial compression failure modes are broadly classified into progressive and global buckling, a distinction that is critical for energy-absorbing applications such as crashworthy components and protective structures. Progressive buckling involves localized, sequential deformation and is highly favorable for energy dissipation due to its ability to sustain load over an extended crushing stroke. This mode typically occurs in two forms: concertina buckling, featuring uniform, axisymmetric folds resembling an accordion, and diamond buckling, characterized by non-axisymmetric, diamond-shaped lobes. Concertina buckling is especially desirable for its stable post-buckling behavior and consistent load plateau, enabling efficient and predictable energy absorption. It is strongly influenced by structural geometry, material properties and the use of triggering mechanisms like grooves or notches to initiate folding. Diamond buckling, while still progressive, often appears in longer or thinner shells and exhibits more complex, less uniform collapse patterns. Despite greater load fluctuations, it still provides substantial energy absorption through plastic deformation, particularly when precise concertina folding is impractical. In contrast, global buckling, such as Euler-type instability, leads to a catastrophic, column-like bending of the entire structure. This failure mode results in a sharp peak followed by a sudden drop in load-carrying capacity, severely limiting energy dissipation. The fundamental difference lies in post-buckling behavior: while progressive modes absorb energy gradually through sequential plastic deformation, global buckling ends abruptly after a single instability event. For this reason, modern energy-absorbing designs prioritize progressive mechanisms especially concertina buckling through optimized geometries, material selection, filler integration, and strategic triggering. Understanding and controlling these distinct collapse modes is essential for achieving high-performance, reliable energy management in advanced structural systems.

The failure modes of the various Z-seam improvements were rigorously visualized and analyzed through a sequential photographic study. For each distinct case comprising the baseline “without improvement” scenario, individual Z-seam improvement techniques, and the synergistic application of both improvement techniques a series of five images was captured at precise deformation distances of 11.2 mm, 22.4 mm, 33.6 mm, 44.8 mm, and 56 mm. This systematic visual documentation allowed for a detailed observation and comparative analysis of the evolving deformation patterns and ultimate failure characteristics across all tested configurations. For each case, a set of images is prepared with the Z-seam position aligned, at the back and nearest, arranged from top to bottom. Figure  4  shows the baseline case without Pressure Advance or the Scarf joint seam, presented from top to bottom as Aligned, Back, and Nearest. Fig. 4 Deformation modes of baseline specimens with Z-seam positions aligned, back and nearest (top to bottom)

The specimen manufactured with an aligned Z-seam configuration demonstrates a catastrophic failure mode governed by the structural integrity of the seam itself. Unlike a ductile collapse, this specimen fails due to a rapid fracture propagation directly along the vertical seam line. Upon initial loading, the specimen begins to deform; however, by the second stage, a vertical crack appears along the Z-seam. As compression increases, this crack rapidly propagates, splitting the specimen in a zipper-like fashion. This delamination halts further plastic deformation and folding. By the final stage, the structure has fully separated, with both halves splaying outward evidence of failure initiated at the seam. This behavior confirms that the aligned Z-seam acts as a critical stress concentrator and structural weakness. Poor interlayer adhesion at the extrusion start-stop point creates a continuous low-strength path prone to failure under tensile hoop stresses, leading to premature, brittle-like collapse. The specimen with the Z-seam positioned at the back exhibits a mixed-mode failure, combining elements of brittle fracture and ductile collapse. Rather than a clean buckle or immediate seam split, failure initiates with interlayer delamination at the contact points with the platens. Subsequent deformation follows an irregular, asymmetric folding pattern, less uniform than typical concertina buckling. In the later stages, the Z-seam becomes a point of weakness, leading to a delayed but less catastrophic seam opening compared to the fully aligned case. This behavior suggests partial energy absorption through non-ideal plastic deformation before seam integrity is lost. While still a weak point, the back-positioned seam allows for greater deformation and structural resistance, likely due to a different stress distribution than the fully aligned configuration. The specimen printed with the ‘nearest’ Z-seam strategy, which randomizes seam locations layer by layer, exhibits a distinct failure mode. By avoiding a continuous vertical seam, it prevents catastrophic splitting and instead fails via progressive buckling. This buckling forms a diamond-shaped lobar pattern, with angled folds collapsing sequentially. However, the process is not entirely ductile localized brittle fractures occur within the folds due to weak inter- and intra-layer adhesion at scattered seam points. The specimen with the Z-seam located at the ‘back’ position exhibits a mixed-mode failure, characterized by initial interlayer delamination at the vertices followed by a combination of buckling and partial seam fracture. The failure sequence commences with visible delamination at the specimen-platen interface, after which the structure undergoes general buckling. Concurrently, a vertical fracture develops along the seam path, though this cleavage is notably less severe than that observed in the fully aligned configuration. This suggests a higher effective adhesion in the ‘back’ position. The improved resistance to splitting may be attributed to the nature of the seam’s path on a curved surface, which is often slightly angled rather than perfectly vertical. This non-linear alignment disrupts the continuity of the weak plane along the print’s axis, providing greater resistance to fracture and allowing for more energy to be absorbed through plastic deformation before the seam’s integrity is ultimately compromised.

As a result, while the global structure deforms progressively, local fractures limit plastic deformation and reduce overall energy absorption. The ‘nearest’ strategy thus avoids catastrophic failure but introduces distributed micro-defects, resulting in a hybrid mode: ductile buckling with localized brittle damage.

Figure  5  shows the specimens with Pressure Advance applied, ordered from top to bottom as Aligned, Back, and Nearest. Despite this adjustment, vertical splits along the Z-seam are still observed. Fig. 5 Deformation modes of Pressure Advance implemented specimens with Z-seam positions aligned, back and nearest (top to bottom)

The specimen fabricated with an aligned Z-seam and optimized with Pressure Advance fails via a mechanism combining general buckling with a dominant brittle fracture, and does not exhibit a folding behavior. Under axial compression, the cylindrical structure undergoes plastic deformation that results in outward radial expansion, or barreling, which in turn generates significant tensile hoop stresses across the specimen’s circumference. Although Pressure Advance improves material adhesion, the aligned seam persists as a primary stress concentrator where these hoop stresses are maximized, causing the initiation and subsequent propagation of a vertical fracture along the seam’s axis. This progressive brittle fracture constitutes the ultimate failure mode for the specimen, preempting the development of any other collapse mechanism and demonstrating that the seam remains the critical structural weakness despite the processing improvements. The ‘nearest’ Z-seam configuration, when combined with Pressure Advance, exhibited progressive folding behavior accompanied by localized splits. Although the randomized seam locations prevent the formation of a continuous vertical weakness, they still act as scattered points of stress concentration. As folding progresses, these regions are susceptible to micro-fractures and surface delaminations. While these small cracks do not merge into a catastrophic split, they compromise structural integrity throughout the deformation process. This behavior indicates that even with optimized extrusion, the ‘nearest’ seam strategy leads to a composite failure mode global ductile buckling consistently accompanied by localized brittle fractures at the dispersed seam sites.

Figure  6  shows the specimens with the Scarf joint seam implemented, ordered from top to bottom as Aligned, Back, and Nearest. While this approach effectively prevented Z-seam splitting, it did not result in a consistent or fully stable folding pattern. Fig. 6 Deformation modes of Scarf Joint Seam–implemented specimens with Z-seam positions aligned, back, and nearest

The implementation of an aligned scarf joint results in a ductile-dominant, mixed-mode failure, representing a significant improvement over all previous configurations. The specimen exhibits no vertical splitting, confirming that the overlapping geometry of the scarf joint effectively distributes tensile hoop stresses and creates a bond at the seam with strength comparable to the bulk material. The primary failure mechanism is progressive buckling, and due to this progressive collapse, the structure has a high tendency to absorb energy. However, the buckling does not proceed in a perfectly uniform manner; instead, the folds develop asymmetrically. This indicates that despite the robust seam, some minor structural heterogeneities persist, leading to a mixed-mode response. Nonetheless, the scarf joint successfully transforms the catastrophic brittle failure of the baseline case into a robust failure mechanism governed primarily by ductile deformation. The specimen featuring a scarf joint at the ‘back’ position exhibited the more ideal failure response of other configurations, characterized by a almost uniform and symmetrical progressive buckling. Consistent with the effectiveness of the scarf joint modification, there was no evidence of splitting or fracture in the implemented region, confirming the high integrity of the bond. This superior performance suggests a beneficial mechanical interaction whereby the modification locally lowers the structure’s rigidity. This localized reduction in stiffness may function as a controlled initiation point for the collapse, promoting a more orderly and symmetrical buckling sequence which, in turn, enhances the structure’s ability to absorb energy in a predictable, fully ductile manner. The ‘nearest’ Z-seam configuration with the scarf joint implemented resulted in a progressive buckling failure that was visibly non-uniform. While the individual scarf joints were robust enough to prevent localized failure at the seam points, their random distribution throughout the specimen’s geometry appears to have created an irregular stress concentration profile. This heterogeneous stress field dictated the subsequent structural collapse, leading to an asymmetric buckling sequence that lacked the high degree of uniformity seen in the ‘back’ scarf joint configuration. This outcome suggests that while strengthening the seam itself is critical, the placement strategy of even a robust seam plays a significant role in determining the uniformity and predictability of the component’s ultimate failure mode.

Figure  7  shows the deformation modes for specimens with both Pressure Advance and the Scarf joint seam, ordered from top to bottom as Aligned, Back, and Nearest. A more uniform and progressive folding behavior is observed when both modification techniques are implemented, resulting in improved energy-absorbing performance. Fig. 7 Deformation modes of specimens incorporating both Pressure Advance and Scarf Joint Seam configurations with Z-seam orientations aligned, back, and nearest

The synergistic application of both Pressure Advance and the scarf joint seam on the aligned configuration results in a significantly enhanced structural response, improving beyond the effects of either individual modification. The specimen fails via a ductile-dominant progressive buckling, characterized by a collapse pattern that approximates a diamond failure mode. Although the collapse is not perfectly symmetrical, this configuration achieves the most uniform folding behavior observed among all test cases. This advanced ductile folding demonstrates that the combined optimization strategy successfully transforms the inherently weak aligned seam into a robust structure capable of a highly controlled, energy-absorbing collapse. The ‘back’ Z-seam configuration with both modifications applied also fails via a mixed-mode progressive buckling, characterized by dominant ductile behavior with no splitting observed at the seam. Although the collapse is visually less uniform than that of the optimized aligned Z-seam specimen, it exhibits a mechanically advantageous characteristic. During compression, this configuration develops a higher number of distinct hinges or folds throughout its structure. This formation of more collapse hinges, despite the lack of perfect symmetry, ultimately results in a superior energy absorption performance. The ‘nearest’ Z-seam configuration with both modifications applied resulted in a non-uniform progressive buckling. A distinguishing feature of this failure mode was the occurrence of localized fragmentation, where small pieces of material were observed to split from the main structure during the collapse. This indicates that while the global failure was ductile, the random distribution of the seam created stress concentrations that led to localized brittle fractures. Despite the non-uniform folding and the presence of fragmentation, the specimen still demonstrated good energy absorbing behavior.

Previous studies investigating FDM-fabricated circular hollow tubes for energy-absorbing applications have reported a wide range of failure modes, strongly dependent on material system, reinforcement strategy, and seam-related defects. Quasi-static compression tests on PETG reinforced with short carbon fibers revealed that the majority of specimens failed at the Z-seam location, where crack initiation and subsequent propagation occurred along the vertical seam line [ 31 ]. Similarly, investigations on PLA circular tubes incorporating an internal concentric ring connected to the outer shell by four radial ribs reported vertical tearing during compression, indicating the presence of dominant axial weakness paths [ 32 ]. In contrast, studies on polyamide (PA) tubes reinforced with glass and carbon fibers demonstrated more progressive collapse behavior: glass fiber–reinforced PA exhibited largely progressive deformation with limited Euler-type buckling, whereas carbon fiber–reinforced PA showed a more stable progressive folding mode [ 33 ]. Additional work on circular tubes fabricated from PLA + , PLA-ST, PLA-LW, PLA-CF, and PETG [ 34 ], as well as PLA-, ABS-, and PETG-based hollow tubular structures produced with conventional slicing strategies, reported predominantly progressive folding behavior under axial compression, despite the presence of unmodified Z-seams [ 30 ]. These observations indicate that progressive collapse can occur in FDM-printed circular tubes, although seam-induced weaknesses often remain a governing factor in failure initiation and variability. In the present study, the baseline specimens fabricated without Z-seam modifications exhibited failure modes consistent with seam-dominated fracture reported in the literature. For both aligned and back seam distributions, failure initiated with the appearance of a vertical crack along the Z-seam during the early stages of loading, followed by rapid crack propagation that split the specimen longitudinally in a zipper-like manner, suppressing progressive folding. In contrast, specimens printed with the nearest seam strategy avoided continuous vertical seam formation and consequently exhibited progressive buckling behavior. The implementation of Pressure Advance alone did not fundamentally alter this trend: seam-dominated fracture persisted for aligned and back distributions, while nearest configurations continued to deform progressively. By comparison, the introduction of the Scarf Joint seam modification resulted in progressive folding behavior across all seam distribution cases, indicating effective disruption of the continuous weak plane at the seam. When both Pressure Advance and Scarf Joint modifications were applied simultaneously, all specimens consistently exhibited stable progressive folding, confirming a synergistic effect in suppressing seam-driven fracture and promoting controlled energy-absorbing deformation.

These findings align well with prior reports and reinforce the conclusion that Z-seam morphology, rather than material alone, plays a decisive role in governing collapse modes in FDM-fabricated circular tubes. By redistributing or geometrically diffusing the seam, the transition from brittle, seam-controlled failure to progressive, energy-efficient folding can be reliably achieved, even without altering the base material system.

sections.heading: Visual examinations
paragraphs: The effect of advanced Z-seam modifications on surface topography and dimensional accuracy was quantified using scan-to-CAD deviation analysis. ABS tubes (15 mm height) were fabricated under each Z-seam condition; the 15 mm height was chosen to ensure unobstructed line-of-sight and adequate depth of field for capturing the inner lumen during 3D scanning. Both inner and outer surfaces were scanned; reconstructed surfaces were rigidly registered to the nominal CAD model, and deviation maps and dimensional metrics were computed; this was performed in Geomagic Control X (3D Systems; trial license). Conformance was reported as the percentage of surface area within a ± 1% tolerance band, along with mean deviation, RMS, and the fractions above/below tolerance. Geometric deviations are tabulated in Table  2 . The software computes, for each measured vertex, the signed distance to its associated reference position on the CAD model; the signed magnitude (the gap distance) is reported as the pointwise deviation. Negative values indicate the scanned geometry lies inside/undersized relative to CAD; positive values indicate it is outside/oversized. Min denotes the most negative deviation (smallest gap), Max the most positive deviation (largest gap), Average the arithmetic mean of all deviations, RMS the root-mean-square deviation, Std. Dev. the standard deviation of deviations, and Var. their variance. The Inside Tolerance (%) metric gives the fraction of points within the user-defined tolerance band (± 1%), quantifying geometric conformance. The tabulated results show clear effects of Z seam strategy on scan to CAD conformance under a ± 1% band. Relative to the baseline without compensation, introducing a scarf joint seam denoted S consistently reduces RMS deviation and increases the percentage of points within the tolerance band. This outcome indicates effective suppression of the localized height step at the layer start and stop. Pressure advance denoted P lowers the share of points that are out of tolerance, which improves dimensional compliance, but produces limited or mixed change in RMS. This pattern implies that flow precompensation mainly mitigates outward drift while the topographic imprint of the seam remains visible in the surface undulation. The combined method denoted PS generally preserves the tolerance benefit and can approach the best overall conformance, although the response of RMS depends on tuning. Practical experience suggests that advance gain, scarf angle and length, seam-adjacent speeds and accelerations, and perimeter count should be co-adjusted to avoid residual micro undulations when both controls are active.

Seam location exerts a secondary influence compared with method selection, but its signatures are informative. Placing the seam at Back typically reduces the maximum positive deviation, which points to a reduction of local material build up where the seam is hidden on the reverse side. The Nearest placement exhibits the lowest minimum values, that is the most negative deviations, which indicates localized inward bias near the area where the seam is parked and heat dissipation is less favorable. Averaged across methods, Back and Aligned locations also reduce the overall out of tolerance share compared with Nearest, while RMS differences among the three placements are modest. This behavior is consistent with location redistributing the imprint toward less critical regions rather than eliminating it.

The decomposition of out of tolerance is dominated by the over tolerance component. The below tolerance share is very small in all cases. This asymmetry reflects a systematic outward bias of the printed geometry. Contributing factors include transient over extrusion at layer initiation and termination, thermal expansion and swelling of deposited filaments before full cooling, and acceleration and jerk dynamics that concentrate small excess material near the seam path. With the chosen registration and projection settings, small alignment errors also tend to manifest as positive distances rather than negative distances, which further reduces the frequency of below tolerance points.

These observations align with the intended mechanisms of the controls. The scarf joint diffuses the seam over an inclined and extended interface, lowering peak local error and improving both RMS and tolerance conformance. Pressure advance anticipates volumetric demand and reduces flow lag and overshoot, which tightens compliance by curbing positive deviations that most often exceed the upper limit. When both are combined in PS, the tolerance benefit is retained but the RMS response becomes sensitive to parameterization, so co-optimization is recommended.

For additively manufactured ABS tubes, the most robust practice is to adopt the scarf joint as the default Z seam strategy to minimize undulation and maximize in tolerance area. Pressure advance should be applied where compliance with the tolerance band is the binding requirement and RMS is already acceptable for function and appearance. The combined PS method is appropriate when both effects are needed, provided that the parameters are calibrated for the specific geometry and toolpath. Where visibility or interface constraints dictate placement, parking the seam at Back provides a practical reduction of the maximum deviation and a lower out of tolerance share with minimal impact on RMS.

Applying both modifications, pressure advance and a scarf seam, resulted in higher energy absorption metrics, as shown in the previous section, with the largest gains observed for the Aligned and Back seam placements. Consistent with the scan to CAD analysis, the Back location provided the second best dimensional accuracy, which limits gap variation and seam induced stress concentrators, stabilizes progressive crushing, and increases specific energy absorption. For energy absorbing hollow tubes, production with pressure advance and a scarf seam, and placement of the Z seam at the Back location, is therefore recommended by this study.

The deviation maps in Fig.  8  illustrate the spatial distribution of scan-to-CAD deviations. Columns encode the Z-seam control: first, neither pressure advance nor scarf joint seam; second, pressure advance; third, scarf joint seam; fourth, both applied. Rows encode seam location: top, Aligned; middle, Back; bottom, Nearest. Fig. 8 Deviation maps of tubes

The maps corroborate the quantitative trends. A scarf-joint seam suppresses the seam-induced height step and, among the single controls, yields the most uniform fields. Pressure advance reduces the extent and intensity of oversize regions, improving tolerance compliance, although a faint inward line texture remains on the inner surface. The combined P–S condition exhibits the cleanest tolerance behavior with minimal exceedances, while Back placement reduces maximum positive deviations and Nearest placement produces the deepest negative deviations. These observations support using a scarf seam as the default strategy for energy-absorbing ABS tubes, adding pressure advance when tighter tolerance compliance is required, and placing the Z-seam at the Back location when feasible.

sections.heading: Statistical analysis of experimental factors
paragraphs: In order to evaluate the statistical significance of the experimental results and quantify the influence of the Z-seam improvement strategies, the compression test data were analyzed using) two-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). This analysis was conducted using Minitab statistical software. The statistical framework was selected to achieve distinct analytical objectives: first, a Main Effects Analysis was performed to isolate and determine the individual influence of the Z-seam Modification and Seam Distribution on the critical mechanical responses (Stiffness, Crush Force Efficiency, Total Absorbed Energy, and Specific Energy Absorption). Second, an Interaction Analysis was conducted to assess the interplay between these factors, determining if the performance of a specific seam modification is statistically dependent on its geometric placement. The detailed statistical decomposition of Stiffness, Crush Force Efficiency, Total Absorbed Energy, and Specific Energy Absorption is summarized in Table  3 . The two-way ANOVA partitions the total experimental variability into contributions arising from the main effects of Modification and Distribution, their interaction, and the residual error. For each source of variation, the sum of squares quantifies the magnitude of variability, which is normalized by the corresponding degrees of freedom to obtain the mean square. The ratio of each factor’s mean square to the error mean square yields the F-statistic, which provides a measure of the strength of the effect relative to experimental noise. Statistical significance is assessed using the associated  p  values, with values below 0.05 indicating a statistically significant effect. In addition, the contribution ratio expresses the proportion of total variance explained by each source, enabling identification of the dominant factors governing mechanical response relative to variability inherent to the experimental process;these statistically signifi cant p-values and dominant variance contributions are highlighted in bold.
