A notable outcome of the two-way ANOVA is the relatively high contribution of the residual error term, particularly for energy-based metrics. While stiffness exhibits a moderate error contribution of 33.5%, the error fraction increases to 62.7%, 65.3%, and 68.2% for CFE, SEA, and EA, respectively. This behavior reflects the fundamentally different deformation mechanisms governing these responses. Stiffness is primarily controlled by initial elastic deformation and global structural geometry, which are highly repeatable under controlled manufacturing conditions. In contrast, EA, SEA, and CFE are governed by progressive collapse phenomena, including localized buckling, interlayer fracture, and plastic hinge formation, which are inherently sensitive to microscale variations in interlayer bonding and filament morphology characteristic of FDM-printed ABS. Consequently, the statistical evaluation of post-yield energy-based metrics is interpreted with appropriate caution and focuses on identifying robust trends that persist despite intrinsic experimental variability.

Among the evaluated responses, stiffness demonstrated the strongest statistical signal. Modification emerged as the dominant control factor (F = 10.94,  p  = 0.0001), explaining 45.9% of the total variance, indicating a variance contribution approximately an order of magnitude greater than the residual noise. Seam Distribution was also statistically significant (F = 4.38,  p  = 0.024), though its contribution was secondary (12.3%).

For Crush Force Efficiency, despite the substantial residual variance (62.7%), Modification remained statistically significant (F = 3.27,  p  = 0.038), accounting for 25.7% of the total variance. This result is mechanically consistent with the stiffness findings, as seam modification governs local rigidity and directly influences the initial peak force, which dominates the efficiency ratio. Seam Distribution was statistically negligible (F = 0.015,  p  = 0.985), contributing only 0.1% of the total variance. Although the interaction term accounted for 11.5% of the variance, it did not achieve statistical significance ( p  = 0.630), indicating that its effect is masked by experimental scatter.

For Total Absorbed Energy and Specific Energy Absorption, neither Modification nor Seam Distribution achieved statistical significance, with low F-values (0.80–1.91) and  p  values exceeding the 0.05 threshold. The controlled factors collectively explain less than 20% of the total variance for both metrics, confirming that energy absorption behavior in these thin-walled structures is dominated by stochastic fracture and collapse processes rather than deterministic seam strategy effects.

While the ANOVA results quantify the statistical significance and relative magnitude of variance contributions, they do not convey the direction or qualitative nature of the observed effects. To facilitate physical interpretation of the printing parameters, the main effects plots presented in Fig.  9  illustrate the mean response at each level of the Modification and Distribution factors. Importantly, these plots remain informative even in the presence of elevated residual variance, as they reflect systematic shifts in the central tendency of the response rather than point-wise variability. Consequently, the main effects plots enable direct visualization of how individual seam strategies influence mechanical performance, complementing the ANOVA findings by clarifying effect directionality and supporting interpretation of statistically robust trends. Fig. 9 Main effects plots for Energy Absorb Metrics

The response for stiffness reveals a clear structural hierarchy driven by seam geometry; the ‘PA’ modification yields the highest mean stiffness (~ 1745 N/mm), indicating that the precise extrusion control reinforces the vertical seam stack against initial compression. Conversely, the ‘Scarf’ strategy results in a sharp reduction in rigidity (~ 1660 N/mm). This suggests that while the tapered joint improves surface finish, the reduced material overlap in the transition zone creates a localized compliance that weakens the structure’s initial elastic response. Regarding distribution, the ‘Aligned’ placement maximizes stiffness by creating a continuous vertical rib, whereas the ‘Nearest’ distribution scatters the discontinuity, effectively interrupting the load path. In contrast, Crush Force Efficiency (CFE) exhibits a distinct binary step-change behavior. The plot shows that both Scarf-based strategies (‘PA and Scarf’ and ‘Scarf’) elevate the mean efficiency from a baseline of ~ 48% to over 50%. This confirms that the primary inhibitor of efficiency is the “seam blob” typical of standard printing; by eliminating this protrusion via the Scarf joint, the initial peak load is blunted, bringing the peak force closer to the mean crushing force, regardless of where the seam is located.

For the energy absorption metrics (EA and SEA), the analysis reveals a notable synergistic trend in the material processing parameters. While ‘PA’ alone or ‘Scarf’ alone result in lower energy absorption compared to the ‘None’ baseline, the combined ‘PA and Scarf’ (Hybrid) modification achieves the highest mean performance across all metrics. This indicates that the mechanisms of Pressure Advance and Scarf Joint are complementary; the PA algorithm compensates for the potential under-extrusion in the Scarf taper, creating a seam that is both geometrically smooth and internally dense. Furthermore, the distribution plot for energy identifies the ‘Back’ position as the optimal seam location. This creates a “geometric shielding” effect: by placing the defect on the face opposite the impactor, the seam is subjected to tensile stresses later in the crushing sequence compared to the ‘Aligned’ or ‘Nearest’ positions, thereby preserving the structural integrity of the primary folding faces for the maximum duration.

To further elucidate the interplay between the printing parameters, the interaction plots presented in Fig.  10  were examined to determine whether the effectiveness of a given seam modification strategy is contingent upon seam distribution. Interpretation of these plots is based on the relative geometry of the response profiles: parallel trends indicate additive and independent effects, whereas non-parallel or intersecting trends suggest potential factor coupling. Fig. 10 Interaction plots for Energy Absorb Metrics

For stiffness, the interaction plot exhibits a localized deviation from strict parallelism, manifested as a rank reversal at the Nearest distribution. While the Pressure Advance (PA) strategy yields the highest stiffness for the Aligned and Back placements, its performance deteriorates markedly when the seam is spatially dispersed, crossing below the None baseline. From a purely visual standpoint, this behavior suggests that the stiffening benefit of PA is sensitive to seam continuity. However, the corresponding interaction term is statistically insignificant ( p  = 0.462), indicating that the observed crossover occurs within overlapping confidence bounds imposed by experimental scatter. Consequently, despite the apparent visual interaction, stiffness remains primarily governed by global seam geometry rather than by a statistically robust coupled mechanism, confirming Modification as the dominant and repeatable control factor.

In the case of Crush Force Efficiency (CFE), the interaction plot displays a pronounced crossover between the high-performing modification strategies. The pure Scarf configuration achieves maximum efficiency at the Aligned position but degrades at the Back location, whereas the Hybrid (PA + Scarf) strategy exhibits the opposite trend, improving at the Back position and surpassing the pure Scarf. This “X-shaped” response indicates a trade-off between peak performance and spatial robustness: the pure Scarf strategy delivers higher nominal efficiency but is more location-sensitive, while the Hybrid modification provides a more stable response across seam placements. Nevertheless, due to the substantial residual variance, this interaction does not reach statistical significance ( p  = 0.630). Mechanistically, this implies that while seam location influences local fold initiation, it does not systematically amplify or suppress the modification effect sufficiently to establish a deterministic interaction.

For Total Absorbed Energy and Specific Energy Absorption, the interaction plots reveal non-parallel trends characterized by a localized maximum associated with the Hybrid–Back configuration. This behavior is consistent with the inherently stochastic nature of post-yield progressive collapse, where localized buckling, interlayer fracture, and crack propagation are highly sensitive to microscale filament morphology and bonding variability. Although the Hybrid–Back combination exhibits an elevated mean response, the absence of statistical significance (p > 0.05) confirms that this behavior cannot be interpreted as a repeatable synergistic interaction. Instead, it represents a potential design preference whose effect is masked by intrinsic process variability.

Overall, the interaction plots are fully consistent with the ANOVA results. While visual features such as rank reversals in stiffness and stability crossovers in CFE are observable, the mechanical response is dominated by main effects rather than statistically validated interactions. For post-yield energy-based metrics in particular, apparent interaction trends are secondary to the inherent experimental variability characteristic of fracture-controlled deformation in FDM-printed thin-walled structures.

sections.heading: Analysis and evaluation of ınput parameter effects on performance metrics using artificial ıntelligence-based machine learning models
paragraphs: In contemporary engineering research, artificial intelligence (AI), particularly through machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) methodologies, has become an essential tool for uncovering intricate, non-linear relationships between input parameters and performance outcomes. Traditional analytical and empirical approaches often struggle to accurately model these interactions, particularly in high-dimensional datasets or scenarios characterized by interdependent variables [ 49 ]. ML algorithms such as decision tree ensembles including Random Forest and CatBoost as well as neural networks, provide robust predictive capabilities by directly learning complex patterns within datasets [ 50 ]. Beyond prediction alone, advancements in explainable AI (XAI) enable deeper interpretability, empowering researchers to understand and quantify each input feature’s contribution to the predicted outcomes. Methods such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), permutation importance, and attention mechanisms in DL architectures offer quantifiable insights into both the relative and directional influence of input variables [ 51 ]. Such interpretability is crucial for enhancing model transparency, optimizing engineering designs, and facilitating data-driven decision-making across critical domains including additive manufacturing, structural optimization, and material selection, where multiple interacting factors influence overall performance [ 52 ].

SHAP is a model-agnostic interpretability framework grounded in cooperative game theory, specifically leveraging Shapley values from economic theory. It assigns importance values to input features based on their contribution to the predictions, effectively calculating the average marginal impact of each feature across all possible combinations. This rigorous mathematical approach ensures a fair attribution of feature influence, enabling researchers to identify key variables and ascertain both the magnitude and direction (positive or negative) of their impacts. Notably, SHAP operates as a post-hoc analytical method, applicable across diverse model types ranging from decision trees to neural networks. Its dual capability of providing local (instance-specific) and global (dataset-wide) explanations renders SHAP exceptionally valuable in engineering contexts where physical interpretability holds equal significance to predictive accuracy. Practical applications include the analysis of material behavior, identification of failure mechanisms, and assessment of structural performance [ 53 ].

CatBoost (Categorical Boosting), developed by Yandex, is a powerful gradient boosting algorithm specifically tailored for structured datasets containing categorical features, a common scenario in engineering applications. Utilizing decision tree ensembles, CatBoost iteratively minimizes a defined loss function, progressively aggregating weak learners into a robust predictive model. One of its primary strengths is the native handling of categorical variables without extensive preprocessing, such as one-hot encoding, thereby simplifying dataset preparation for materials classification, cross-sectional geometry categorization, and process parameter modeling. CatBoost employs Ordered Boosting to systematically reduce overfitting risks by sequentially organizing data subsets for each iteration, complemented by robust L2 regularization techniques to enhance generalization. These characteristics make CatBoost particularly advantageous for analyzing small, experimentally constrained datasets. Additionally, its seamless integration with SHAP analysis facilitates detailed interpretability alongside accurate predictions, providing comprehensive insights into the influences of design parameters and material properties on engineering outcomes [ 54 ].

In this study, CatBoost regression combined with SHAP analysis was employed to systematically examine the effects of basic slicing parameters specifically Z-seam distributions (aligned, back, nearest) and advanced slicing parameters, namely Pressure Advance and Scarf Joint Seam implementations, both individually and collectively, on the energy absorption characteristics of 3D-printed thin-walled circular polymeric tubes. Following comprehensive data cleaning and validation, which included group-wise statistical comparisons to discern fundamental performance trends, the model was trained using one-hot encoding to represent categorical variables clearly and effectively.

Regularized CatBoost models were developed for each performance metric, including Specific Energy Absorption (SEA), Stiffness, Crushing Force Efficiency (CFE), and Absorbed Energy, and validated through Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). LOOCV is particularly beneficial for smaller datasets, maximizing data utilization while providing a reliable estimate of generalization performance [ 55 ]. SHAP values were subsequently calculated to quantify both the relative importance and directional influence of each input feature.

Under the adopted cross-validation protocol, the predictive performance of the regression models was evaluated using variance-based and error-based metrics for absorbed energy (EA), stiffness, specific energy absorption (SEA), and crush force efficiency (CFE). The resulting coefficients of determination (R 2 ) were 0.32 for absorbed energy, 0.66 for stiffness, 0.34 for SEA, and 0.37 for CFE. Root mean square error (RMSE) values were 9.58 for absorbed energy, 42.56 for stiffness, 0.69 for SEA, and 2.36 for CFE, corresponding to relative RMSE values of 4.2%, 2.5%, 4.2%, and 4.8%, respectively. Mean absolute errors (MAE) were 7.96, 34.50, 0.57, and 1.78, while mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) were 3.52%, 2.03%, 3.53%, and 3.64% for EA, stiffness, SEA, and CFE, respectively.

The coefficient of determination (R 2 ) quantifies the proportion of the total observed variance in the response variable that is explained by the model; higher R 2  values indicate stronger explanatory power, while low values reflect either model limitations or, more commonly in post-yield responses, high intrinsic experimental scatter. Because R 2  is variance-based, it is particularly sensitive to stochastic fluctuations and between-sample variability. In contrast, the root mean square error (RMSE) measures the typical magnitude of the prediction error in the original physical units of the response and therefore provides a direct indication of absolute predictive accuracy; lower RMSE values correspond to more accurate predictions. To enable comparison across response metrics with different magnitudes, the percentage RMSE (%RMSE) normalizes RMSE by the mean response level, yielding a scale-independent indicator of prediction accuracy, with smaller values indicating better model performance. The mean absolute error (MAE) represents the average absolute difference between predicted and measured values and, like RMSE, is expressed in the same units as the target variable; lower MAE values indicate closer agreement between predictions and observations. Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) further quantifies predictive accuracy by averaging the absolute percentage deviation between predicted and experimental values across all samples. Expressed as a percentage, MAPE is scale-free and lower values indicate greater accuracy. According to the Lewis benchmark [ 56 ,  57 ], MAPE values below 10% correspond to highly accurate forecasting, values between 10 and 20% indicate good forecasting, values between 20 and 50% represent reasonable forecasting, and values exceeding 50% are considered inaccurate.

For stiffness, the model achieves a moderate-to-strong fit (R 2  = 0.66) combined with very low RMSE (2.5%) and MAPE (2.03%), indicating that both variance capture and absolute predictive accuracy are high. Consequently, SHAP attributions for stiffness are considered robust for identifying dominant parameters and their directional influence. For absorbed energy and SEA, R 2  values are comparatively low (≈0.32–0.34), reflecting the dominance of residual variability associated with stochastic post-yield deformation mechanisms, including localized buckling, interlayer fracture, and crack propagation. Nevertheless, the corresponding RMSE and MAPE values remain below 5%, demonstrating that the models accurately predict the central tendency of these responses despite limited variance explanation. Accordingly, SHAP results for EA and SEA remain informative for identifying influential factors and qualitative trends, although effect magnitudes should be interpreted with caution.

A similar behavior is observed for CFE, where R 2  = 0.37 reflects the compounded variability inherent to this metric, which is defined as a ratio of peak and mean crushing forces and therefore amplifies experimental noise. Despite this, the low RMSE (4.8%) and MAPE (3.64%) indicate accurate estimation of the overall performance level. Following the Lewis benchmark, all MAPE values fall within the “highly accurate forecasting” regime (< 10%), confirming strong absolute predictive performance across all response metrics. The apparent discrepancy between low R 2  and low percentage-based error metrics therefore arises from the predominance of irreducible experimental scatter rather than from model inadequacy. As a result, the developed models are well suited for estimating mean structural performance and extracting physically meaningful trends, while fine-scale discrimination between closely spaced experimental groups remains limited by intrinsic process variability.

The trends identified through the SHAP-based regression analysis are fully consistent with the statistical structure revealed by the two-way ANOVA. In the ANOVA results, stiffness exhibited the lowest residual error contribution and the strongest main-effect dominance, indicating a largely deterministic response governed by seam modification and distribution. This behavior is directly reflected in the regression performance, where stiffness achieved the highest R 2  alongside very low RMSE and MAPE values, confirming both strong variance explanation and high absolute predictive accuracy. In contrast, absorbed energy, SEA, and CFE were characterized in the ANOVA by dominant residual error contributions (> 60%), reflecting the stochastic nature of post-yield collapse mechanisms in FDM-printed structures. Correspondingly, the regression models for these metrics yielded comparatively low R 2  values, indicating limited variance capture, while maintaining low RMSE and MAPE values that confirm accurate prediction of mean response levels. This convergence of ANOVA and regression evidence demonstrates that the reduced explanatory power for energy-based metrics is driven by irreducible experimental scatter rather than model inadequacy. Consequently, both analyses consistently support the interpretation that stiffness is governed by robust, repeatable geometric effects, whereas post-yield performance metrics are dominated by intrinsic variability, for which SHAP-derived trends remain physically meaningful but should be interpreted at a qualitative or trend-based level rather than as precise quantitative predictors.

The SHAP analysis outcomes were visualized through comparative bar charts, clearly depicting the relative contributions of basic and advanced slicing parameters to each energy absorption metric. Additionally, SHAP heatmaps were created to elucidate the individual and combined effects of parameter selections on performance, identifying slicing parameters that positively or negatively influenced energy absorption behavior. The analytical insights derived from the model closely corresponded with experimental results, providing a robust, data-driven framework for understanding and optimizing slicing parameter interactions and their impact on energy absorption performance.

The relative importance of Z-seam distribution and advanced Z-seam modification on various energy absorption metrics was quantified using SHAP-based feature importance analysis. The comparative bar chart presented in Fig.  11  provides clear insight into this critical research question, revealing whether basic slicing parameters or advanced slicing modifications serve as the dominant design variable for each mechanical performance indicator. Fig. 11 Relative ımportance of Z-seam modification versus Z-Seam distribution on performance metrics

The SHAP-based feature importance analysis reveals distinct trends in how basic and advanced Z-seam parameters influence energy absorption metrics. For total absorbed energy, the basic Z-seam distribution defined by the placement of the seam (aligned, back, nearest) emerges as the dominant factor, accounting for 55.1% of the overall importance, whereas advanced modification techniques contribute 44.9%. This underscores that the spatial distribution of the seam plays a more critical role in determining the structure’s energy absorption capacity during compression. In contrast, stiffness is predominantly governed by advanced Z-seam modifications, such as Pressure Advance and Scarf Joint, which collectively represent 67.9% of the importance, compared to only 32.1% for the basic distribution. This finding highlights the necessity of advanced seam control for applications requiring enhanced structural rigidity. For specific energy absorption (SEA), both parameter categories exert considerable influence, with advanced modifications having a slightly higher impact (53.3%) than basic distribution (46.7%). This suggests that an optimal SEA can be achieved by simultaneously tuning both the seam placement and implementing advanced modifications. Finally, crushing force efficiency (CFE) is overwhelmingly dictated by advanced Z-seam modifications, which account for 79.8% of the importance, leaving only 20.2% to basic seam distribution. Therefore, maximizing CFE is contingent upon the effective deployment of advanced seam techniques, rather than simple alterations of the seam location.

The directional SHAP heatmap presented in Fig.  12  offers detailed insights into the effects of slicing parameters on specific energy absorption metrics by visualizing the average impact of each parameter on model predictions. In this visualization, blue cells indicate a negative influence, signifying that the parameter decreases the value of the target metric, whereas red cells denote a positive influence, reflecting a increase in performance. The intensity of the color corresponds to the strength of the effect, while the numerical values within each cell represent the average SHAP magnitude where larger absolute values indicate a stronger impact on the predicted metric. Fig. 12 Average Directional SHAP impact of each modification on target metrics

Among all evaluated metrics, stiffness is the parameter most strongly influenced by Z-seam mitigation strategies, indicating that slicing modifications have a particularly pronounced effect on the structural rigidity of the printed tubes. This is followed by absorbed energy, which also shows notable sensitivity to slicing conditions. In contrast, both SEA and CFE exhibit relatively minor variations across the tested parameters. For absorbed energy, the Back seam distribution emerges as the most influential, positively affecting the metric, while Pressure Advance also contributes favorably, and the Nearest seam distribution has a negative impact. In the case of stiffness, the Scarf Joint Seam modification leads to a substantial reduction, followed by a pronounced decrease with the Nearest distribution, whereas the Aligned distribution and Pressure Advance both enhance stiffness. The Back distribution has minimal influence on stiffness. For SEA, the Nearest distribution slightly decreases values, while all other parameters have modest positive effects. With respect to CFE, the Aligned distribution exerts a slight negative influence, while other parameters particularly the Scarf Joint Seam contribute positively. Taken together, these results suggest that combining Pressure Advance and Scarf Joint Seam modifications, while avoiding the Nearest seam distribution and favoring the Back distribution, is the optimal strategy for achieving a balance of moderate stiffness and improved energy absorption in FDM-fabricated structures.

To explicitly correlate the empirical findings with the statistical feature importance derived from the machine learning model, Table  4  presents a synthesis of the optimal experimental conditions alongside the primary algorithmic drivers. To establish a rigorous connection between these domains, the quantities reported in the summary table are defined as follows. The Optimal Experimental Combination corresponds to the slicing-parameter configuration that yielded the maximum measured value of the given response metric among all tested specimens. Complementing this, the ‘Dominant SHAP Variable’ is identified from the trained regression model as the input feature with the highest mean absolute SHAP value, indicating the parameter that contributes most strongly, on average, to the model’s predictions. The associated ‘Importance (%)’ is obtained by normalizing the mean absolute SHAP value of this dominant variable by the sum of mean absolute SHAP values across all input features, thereby expressing its contribution as a fraction of the total explainable model influence. Finally, the ‘Directional Impact’ is determined from the sign of the average SHAP value of the dominant variable when that feature is active; a positive sign indicates that the parameter increases the predicted response, while a negative sign indicates a reducing effect. Together, these definitions establish a transparent framework for directly comparing the experimentally optimal designs with the statistically most influential parameters identified by the SHAP analysis. Building on this framework, the results summarized in Table  4  reveal a clear and physically consistent correspondence between experimentally observed optimal designs and the dominant drivers identified by the SHAP analysis. For Stiffness, the experimentally optimal configuration (Aligned + Pressure Advance) achieves maximum rigidity by excluding the Scarf Joint, a finding directly corroborated by SHAP: the Scarf Joint Seam is identified as the dominant variable (54.0% importance) with a distinct Negative (−) directional impact, quantifying the compliance penalty introduced by the tapered overlap. In contrast, Absorbed Energy is maximized by the ‘Back + Pressure Advance + Scarf Joint Seam’ combination, which is reflected in SHAP identifying Pressure Advance as the dominant variable (29.5%) with a Positive (+) contribution, underscoring its role in promoting extrusion consistency during progressive deformation. Similarly, for Crush Force Efficiency (CFE), the optimal experimental configuration (Back + Scarf Joint Seam) aligns with the SHAP attribution, which assigns the largest share of importance (60.8%) to the Scarf Joint Seam with a Positive (+) impact, confirming that the scarf geometry effectively smooths the crushing plateau. Although these energy-based metrics exhibit higher intrinsic variability,the consistency between the empirically optimal combinations and the SHAP-derived dominant variables supported by Mean Absolute Percentage Errors (MAPE) consistently below 4% indicates that the machine learning model successfully captures the systematic trends governing mean performance. Consequently, Table [X] provides a concise synthesis that links empirical optimization with statistically interpretable parameter effects, reinforcing the complementary nature of the experimental, ANOVA, and SHAP-based analyses.

A direct comparison of the ANOVA variance decomposition and the SHAP-based effect analysis demonstrates strong internal consistency and clear methodological complementarity. ANOVA assesses whether the influence of printing parameters is statistically resolvable relative to experimental scatter, whereas SHAP decomposes the explainable component of the regression model to identify dominant parameters and the direction of their effects on the mean response. For normalized stiffness, both approaches converge unequivocally: ANOVA identifies Z-seam modification as the dominant and highly significant factor (45.9% contribution,  p  = 0.0001), while SHAP independently attributes the majority of predictive importance (67.9%) to advanced seam strategies, confirming stiffness as a largely deterministic response governed by seam geometry and extrusion control. A similar convergence is observed for crush force efficiency (CFE), where ANOVA confirms modification as the only statistically significant factor despite substantial residual variance, and SHAP assigns 79.8% of total importance to seam modification, indicating that the mean efficiency level remains primarily controlled by modification-induced regulation of peak force. In contrast, for total absorbed energy (EA) and specific energy absorption (SEA), ANOVA shows that controlled factors fail to achieve statistical significance and that residual error exceeds 65%, reflecting the dominance of stochastic post-yield collapse mechanisms rather than the absence of systematic parameter effects. ANOVA therefore reaches its inferential limit for these responses, as factor-induced variance is insufficiently large relative to noise. Within a predictive framework, however, SHAP still reveals how the predictable fraction of EA and SEA is structured, identifying seam distribution as the dominant contributor for EA (55.1%) and a more balanced contribution for SEA. Consequently, SHAP does not contradict ANOVA but complements it by elucidating relative importance and directional tendencies within the bounds imposed by experimental variability; deterministic seam control governs stiffness and peak-force-related efficiency, whereas energy absorption metrics remain intrinsically noise-dominated and should be interpreted qualitatively rather than as statistically resolved effects.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Advanced Z-seam control is demonstrated to systematically and reproducibly reshape both dimensional fidelity and the crushing response of FDM-printed ABS circular tubes. Among the evaluated crashworthiness metrics, initial stiffness emerges as the most sensitive response, exhibiting a clear dependence on Z-seam strategy. Stiffness decreases when the Scarf Joint seam and Nearest seam placement are employed, while it increases under Pressure Advance and under Aligned and Back placements, with Back performing at least equivalently to Aligned. This confirms that seam-related extrusion dynamics directly govern the early elastic–plastic response under axial loading.

A metric-resolved analysis reveals distinct governing levers for different performance objectives. Total absorbed energy is influenced more strongly by seam placement than by seam modification, with Back placement consistently yielding the highest energy absorption, followed by Aligned and Nearest. In contrast, stiffness is controlled primarily by the seam modification strategy rather than by placement. Specific energy absorption is dominated by seam modification and reaches its maximum when Pressure Advance and the Scarf Joint seam are applied simultaneously. Crush force efficiency is likewise significantly more sensitive to seam modification than to placement, indicating that local seam geometry and extrusion pressure control strongly affect load uniformity during progressive collapse.

These trends are consistent with the underlying physical mechanisms. Pressure Advance enhances interlayer bonding continuity and suppresses localized over-extrusion at seam initiation and termination, thereby increasing stiffness and promoting stable folding. The Scarf Joint seam redistributes the Z-seam discontinuity over an inclined overlap, reducing local material buildup and root-mean-square surface deviation, which intentionally lowers stiffness while enabling more regular and controlled folding. When combined, Pressure Advance and the Scarf Joint seam deliver the most favorable crash response, characterized by reduced peak crushing force, elevated mean crushing force, and the highest specific energy absorption particularly when the seam is placed at the Back location. Seam placement nevertheless remains influential: Back placement consistently improves absorbed energy, specific energy absorption, and dimensional tolerance behavior, whereas Nearest placement reduces stiffness and promotes distributed micro-defects that fragment under compressive loading.

Dimensional metrology independently confirms these mechanical trends. Specimens produced without any Z-seam mitigation exhibit the lowest proportion of surface geometry within the ± 1% tolerance band. All mitigation strategies increase dimensional compliance, with the Scarf Joint seam producing the most substantial improvement in in-tolerance surface area. Pressure Advance alone yields more modest gains in overall tolerance compliance, despite its effectiveness in suppressing oversize regions and increasing stiffness, highlighting a clear trade-off between dimensional conformity and mechanical rigidity.

The combined statistical and machine learning analyses provide complementary insight into these behaviors. Two-way ANOVA revealed that, for highly variable post-yield responses such as absorbed energy and specific energy absorption, factor contributions are partially masked by intrinsic experimental scatter, limiting the statistical resolvability of main effects despite clear directional trends. In contrast, stiffness and crush force efficiency exhibited stronger statistical sensitivity to Z-seam modification strategies.

To interrogate these relationships beyond variance-based inference, gradient-boosted regression models were employed and validated using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation. While coefficient of determination (R 2 ) values remained moderate for energy-based metrics reflecting the inherently stochastic nature of progressive fracture the models achieved consistently low Mean Absolute Percentage Errors (below 4%) and relative RMSE values below 5%. This confirms high predictive fidelity for central performance tendencies despite irreducible experimental variability.

SHAP-based attribution bridges this gap by resolving relative parameter importance independent of strict statistical significance. Seam placement was identified as the dominant contributor to absorbed energy, whereas seam modification strategy governed stiffness and crush force efficiency. These findings explain why ANOVA alone cannot fully characterize contribution pathways for SEA and EA, while SHAP analysis successfully reveals their governing process variables.

From an optimization perspective consistent with Structural and Multidisciplinary Optimization frameworks, Z-seam modification and seam placement function as discrete design variables within a multi-objective design space. SHAP-informed ranking enables an efficient navigation toward a non-dominated solution set that balances dimensional accuracy, moderated peak force, elevated mean crushing force, and high specific energy absorption. Within this Pareto-optimal space, the combined application of Pressure Advance and the Scarf Joint seam with Back seam placement emerges as the most balanced solution, simultaneously maximizing specific energy absorption while achieving the highest dimensional compliance. This configuration therefore represents the optimal compromise between crash energy absorption and dimensional accuracy for FDM-printed ABS circular tubes under the investigated conditions.

For practical engineering implementation, the Scarf Joint seam should be adopted as the reference strategy when dimensional compliance and fold regularity are prioritized; Pressure Advance should be introduced when higher stiffness and tighter control of oversize deviations are required; and Back seam placement should be preferred for energy-absorbing components. Through coordinated tuning of Pressure Advance gain, Scarf Joint geometry, and local deposition paths near the seam, Z-seam management transitions from a cosmetic slicing choice into a quantifiable, optimization-ready design variable capable of delivering robust, lightweight crash elements suitable for safety–critical applications.
